title: Staffed Junk Playgrounds as Apartment Amenity
one_liner: Adventure playgrounds with loose parts, dirt, tools and trained playworkers, installed on unused lots at family-heavy apartment communities and sold to landlords as a renewal lever.
customer: Owners and operators of garden-style, suburban and build-to-rent multifamily communities (200+ units, many households with children ages 5-12). Parents are the secondary payers via optional drop-in fees.
problem: Roughly 40 states now require schools to restrict phones, yet the 3-6pm window at home is where screen time actually happens. Australia's under-16 social media ban has reportedly changed daily use only slightly (about 58% still use daily vs about 60% before), a sign that removing a device without providing somewhere to go does little. Parents want unsupervised, physical, unstructured play but fear liability and have no safe place. Meanwhile landlords spend amenity budgets on gyms and coworking rooms nobody uses and lose family tenants to turnover that costs thousands of dollars per unit.
solution: A turnkey adventure playground service in the UK 'playwork' tradition: pallets, tires, rope, cardboard, sand, water, hammers and a supervised fire pit on an old parking lot or lawn, run 15-20 hours a week (after school and weekends) by trained playworkers who intervene as little as possible. The operator supplies the loose-parts kit, a written risk-benefit assessment, staff training, a background-check protocol and a specialty liability policy. The property signs a monthly contract, and families pay nothing or a small add-on. Tracked outcomes include tenant survey scores and renewal rates for families with school-age children.
why_now: Phone-free school laws spread across about 40 states by mid-2026 and the 'anxious generation' framing turned play-based childhood into a mainstream parenting goal. Free-range parenting statutes in a growing number of states reduce neglect-law fear. Build-to-rent operators are competing on amenities and retention. Nonprofit adventure playgrounds exist but cannot scale because of staffing and liability, which a landlord-funded model solves.
revenue_model: Service contract of about $3-5k per property per month (staff, materials, insurance, management), optional $15-20 per child drop-in for non-residents, and multi-property master agreements with regional operators. Ten properties gives roughly $400-600k in annual recurring revenue.
non_obvious_insight: The real buyer of 'screen-free childhood' is the landlord, not the parent. One prevented move-out saves thousands of dollars in turnover, so a single retained family pays for a month of the program, and kids' friendships create lock-in that no gym can. The barrier to adventure playgrounds was never demand, it was insurance and staffing, and packaging them as a managed property service turns a nonprofit hobby into infrastructure.
first_30_days: Find one friendly 300-unit community and offer an 8-week free trial in exchange for data. Spend about $2k on pallets, tires, rope and tools, hire two playwork or early-childhood students, and get a liability quote from a specialty broker. Survey tenants with kids before and after, and track leasing-team feedback. Photograph everything and pitch 20 regional property managers through local apartment associations and LinkedIn. Aim to convert the trial and one more property to paid contracts within 4-5 months.

title: Contingency Royalty Audits for Game Developers
one_liner: A $99 automated statement check that finds provable underpayments in publisher royalty reports, then hands winnable cases to forensic accountants on contingency.
customer: Developers signed with publishers who are unrecouped or getting opaque quarterly statements. They pay $99-299 for the check and 20-25% of any recovered money. Referral fees also come from games lawyers and auditors.
problem: Audit clauses exist in most publishing deals (one analysis found them in 88% of deals with an advance), but a formal audit costs more than a small studio can recover, so publishers effectively face none. One 30-contract analysis found 42% gave the publisher 100% of revenue until recoupment. Marketing 'recoupables', vague net-revenue definitions, cross-collateralization and FX and VAT handling all hide errors. Devs sit on a spreadsheet they can't verify.
solution: Devs upload the contract and statements. We rebuild the recoup waterfall from the contract's own definitions and compare it with independent signals: review-count unit estimates, price history and regional mix. We flag anomalies such as marketing above a cap, taxes deducted twice, giveaway keys counted as spend, and FX gaps. A clause pack and a negotiation script push new deals toward Steamworks read-only financial permission for the dev. Flagged cases go to a panel of forensic accountants who send a formal audit notice.
why_now: The 2023-25 layoffs pushed thousands of devs into 'marketing-only' publishing deals with recoup terms. LLMs can now parse contracts and statements at near-zero marginal cost. Funding is tight, so every unpaid royalty matters.
revenue_model: Flat pre-audit fee, 20-25% contingency on recoveries (cheaper than the roughly 40% litigation contingency), and referral fees from lawyers. Later: a paid tier for funds and lenders that want portfolio royalty monitoring.
non_obvious_insight: Detection was never the bottleneck. Cost was. A cheap pre-audit that separates provable errors from noise lets an auditor take only winnable cases. Publishers in a small, gossipy industry often settle quickly once a credible notice lands, because they don't want the precedent to spread, and many errors are honest spreadsheet mistakes.
first_30_days: Launch a free recoup-waterfall calculator and a 'publisher-deal red-flag scan' on r/gamedev and dev Discords. Collect about 100 anonymized statements as training and proof data. Sign referral deals with two games-industry lawyers and one forensic accountant. Take the first 5 contingency cases with flagged anomalies over $10k.

title: Weather Forecasts for GPS Jamming
one_liner: A crowd-sensed, forecastable map of GNSS jamming and spoofing for the civil operators nobody warns: survey and RTK fleets, drone operators and marine underwriters.
customer: First: commercial drone operators, RTK survey and construction machine-control fleets, and precision-ag contractors in the Baltics, Poland, Finland, Turkey and the Gulf, at $99 to $499 a month. Second: marine war-risk MGAs, P&I clubs and route planners, at $50k to $250k a year.
problem: Jamming and spoofing have surged (EASA revised its GNSS-interference bulletin again in July 2026; Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb dominate ship incidents; insurers are bracing for mega-claims). Operators learn about it when a drone flies away or autosteer fails. Public maps such as GPSJam are daily averages built from ADS-B, too coarse for a specific field or route hour.
solution: A sensor network of cheap multi-band GNSS receivers and opted-in Android raw-GNSS phones (hosts are farmers, truckers and drone pilots, paid in free forecasts). It detects carrier-to-noise collapse and spoofing signatures at about 1 km resolution in near real time. On top of that sits a forecast (jammers repeat by hour and geometry) and an API/SMS alert such as 'L1 degraded within 20 km of your flight plan 14:00-16:00'. A signed position-integrity report is offered to insurers.
why_now: Dual-frequency GNSS chips cost about $10 and expose raw measurements. Android exposes raw GNSS data. Jamming intensity rose sharply through 2025-26, and insurers and P&I clubs have started buying authentication tech, so the demand signal is visible in the market.
revenue_model: SaaS of $99 to $999 a month for fleets. Annual data licences of $50k to $250k to insurers and MGAs. Per-report fee for integrity certificates. Optional hardware host kit sold at cost.
non_obvious_insight: Jamming is spatially and temporally patterned like weather, so it can be forecast, not just mapped afterward. The paying buyers are not militaries but civil operators whose exposure nobody prices. The sensor network gets built for free if you pay hosts in forecasts.
first_30_days: Deploy 30 receivers with three agri-drone and survey firms in Poland and the Baltics. Email a weekly jamming map overlaid on their own flight logs. Sign 10 paying users at 99 EUR a month. Send a route-level sample dataset to two marine war-risk underwriters.

title: Year-Three Warranty Claims Agent and Failure Index
one_liner: An agent that files manufacturer, retailer and credit-card extended-warranty claims when your stuff dies, paid on success, whose claims data becomes a durability index that Amazon's star ratings cannot provide.
customer: Consumers who bought $200 to $3,000 durables (appliances, e-bikes, laptops, mattresses, power tools) in the past 1 to 4 years. Later data buyers: home-warranty and insurance firms, retailers, brand quality teams and AI shopping agents.
problem: Amazon's incentives end at the return window, and reviews freeze at week two, but failures happen in year two to four. The money left behind sits in three layers: manufacturer warranties, retailer protection plans and credit-card extended warranty. It goes unclaimed because people cannot find the receipt, do not know which layer applies, or quit at the phone tree. Meanwhile shoppers have no independent durability signal, and the one consumer tool for spotting fake reviews, Fakespot, was shut down by Mozilla in July 2025 for lack of a business model.
solution: The consumer connects a receipt source (read-only, receipts only, opt-in) and the agent builds a coverage ledger for big purchases: warranty end dates, card-benefit eligibility, retailer plan status. When the user texts that the dishwasher died, the agent assembles the claim packet (receipt, serial number, photos, symptom), files with the right layer over email, chat or a voice agent, and chases it to resolution. Every outcome (brand, model, failure mode, age at failure) goes into an anonymized Failure Index.
why_now: LLM agents can now read messy receipts and run multi-channel claims at a cost per claim low enough for a success-fee model. AI shopping assistants and agentic checkout need trustworthy durability signals, which star ratings do not supply. Fakespot's 2025 shutdown proved consumers will not pay to check reviews, so the payer has to be the claim recovery itself.
revenue_model: A success fee of 20% to 25% of recovered value (refund, repair or replacement), or $19 flat per filed claim. In year two, license the Failure Index by API or report to warranty administrators, insurers, retailers and shopping agents ($2k to $25k per month). Affiliate referrals for a better replacement at the moment of failure.
non_obvious_insight: The unowned moment in commerce is month 25, not the purchase. Every incumbent (Amazon, brands, card issuers) profits when claiming is hard, and a failure someone bothered to claim is a labeled ground-truth data point, unlike a star rating. Sell claims recovery to consumers, who will pay, and the byproduct dataset is what the institutions that price durability will pay for.
first_30_days: Run it concierge-style. Put up a landing page: 'Did your appliance, e-bike or laptop die within 3 years? We file the claim, you pay only if we recover.' Recruit 30 claimants from Reddit (r/appliances, r/ebikes) and local Facebook groups. Draft claims with an LLM and send them by hand, logging every outcome. Pick one category (for example e-bike batteries or robot vacuums) and publish five public posts on what the claims data shows. Approach one home-warranty or appliance-retail company for a paid data pilot.

title: Under-Canopy Grave Detection Survey Service
one_liner: Find unmarked graves before the bulldozer does, using drone LiDAR that sees through trees, machine-learning triage and targeted ground-penetrating radar.
customer: Municipalities, state DOTs, developers, title companies, utilities and solar or pipeline builders, plus churches and heritage nonprofits.
problem: Lost and unrecorded burial grounds are usually discovered when earthmovers hit them, causing delay, cost and heartbreak. Historic cemeteries, especially those of marginalized communities, are often undocumented. GPR surveys are slow, costly per acre and limited by scarce operators. There is no burial-risk layer in due diligence.
solution: Drone LiDAR and photogrammetry across large tracts to detect depressions and anomalies under canopy, ML-ranked into a probability map, followed by targeted GPR verification of the top candidates. Deliver a survey report and a registry entry. Add LLM reading of handwritten cemetery and church records.
why_now: Survey-grade drone LiDAR is now cheap, ML for GPR and terrain anomalies has matured, and rural land is being cleared quickly for solar, data centers and pipelines. LLMs can now read handwritten historic records. Everstory's drone mapping of about 400 cemeteries shows the method works for known sites.
revenue_model: $200-$1,500 per acre depending on terrain and depth, annual subscriptions for DOTs and utilities, and data licensing to title insurers.
non_obvious_insight: Every earthmoving project carries burial-risk liability that appears in no database. The same survey serves developers, heritage groups and families, so it can be financed by the party with the most to lose.
first_30_days: Pilot with 2 churches or heritage groups on grant-funded work. Rent a LiDAR drone and pitch 5 solar developers on due-diligence add-ons. Recruit a GPR contractor and a cultural-resources archaeologist for sign-off.

title: Escaped-Burn Liability Cover Verified From Orbit
one_liner: Go/no-go data and liability cover for prescribed burn associations, priced from fuel dryness and settled by satellite proof that the fire never left the unit.
customer: Prescribed burn associations, contract burn bosses and private landowners (ranchers, forest owners) in Texas, Oklahoma, the Great Plains, the Southeast, Colorado and the West Coast. Surplus-lines MGAs, insurers and state forestry agencies are the second customer.
problem: Prescribed fire is the cheapest wildfire-adaptation tool, but escaped-fire liability cover is described as 'unavailable, unaffordable and vital' in places like Oregon and Colorado. Only a few risk pools exist, such as three Georgia burn associations with about 1,600 members. Insurers cannot price it because after an escape nobody has objective evidence of what was burned or when.
solution: Phase 1 is a software and certificate business that needs no insurance licence. A per-burn pack combines satellite live fuel-moisture and soil-dryness signals with forecasts as a documented go/no-go. A 72-hour containment certificate compares thermal hotspots (VIIRS, FireSat, commercial thermal) and next-day burn-scar perimeter (Sentinel-2 and Landsat at 10-30 m) against the permitted unit. Phase 2 has a partner MGA or risk retention group underwrite association pools, with verification making claims close to binary.
why_now: FireSat's first three operational satellites (July 2026) will deliver at least twice-daily data to early adopters by end-2026, heading to about 20 satellites and hourly revisit by 2029. Suppression backlogs and insurance retreat are pushing states to legalise more burning, and the Nov-Apr burn season starts within weeks. New free 10-30 m optical and radar archives make unit-level perimeter checks nearly free to produce.
revenue_model: $95-$250 per burn certificate plus $1.50-$3 per acre. Association memberships of $1-3K/yr. Later, MGA commission or a data licence to insurers underwriting pools.
non_obvious_insight: Prescribed fire is uninsurable not because it is risky but because nobody can prove afterwards that it stayed inside the line. An objective, cheap orbital perimeter check turns an unpriceable moral-hazard argument into an auditable event. Gross-negligence liability standards in state burn laws turn on documented preparation, which the go/no-go pack supplies.
first_30_days: Offer free winter-season pilots to 10 burn associations (TX, OK, NE, GA, CO) and build the containment check on free VIIRS, Sentinel-2 and Landsat data while applying for FireSat early-adopter access. Start charging $95 per certificate from December. Get one surplus-lines broker or MGA to review the certificate format as the seed of a Phase 2 pool.

title: Leak-Proof Outsourcing Passport for Game Studios
angle: Pairing 2: Gaming, entertainment, live experiences, fandoms x Cybersecurity, deepfake fraud, identity verification, scams targeting consumers and businesses
one_liner: Contractor identity checks at first build access, per-recipient build watermarking and reusable vendor security attestations for the outsourcing chain (art, audio, QA, porting) that leaks unreleased games.
customer: Mid-size and AA/indie publishers that outsource to 20-200 external vendors. Also the vendors themselves (art studios in Poland, Vietnam, India and elsewhere, QA houses, localization and voice studios, freelance marketplaces) who need a portable credential to win work.
problem: Layoffs and cost-cutting push more production to external vendors and freelancers. Per the briefing, Ubisoft headcount fell from 18,666 to 16,590 and EA's $55B buyout, which closed 4 Aug 2026, aims to cut operating costs by putting AI throughout. Each vendor has weaker security than the publisher while unreleased builds are the crown jewels (GTA VI launches 19 Nov 2026, and past leaks like Rockstar 2022, Insomniac 2023 and Game Freak 2024 show the pattern). Remote contractors are also prime targets for identity fraud: North Korean IT-worker schemes hit 'nearly 70' and 'over 100' US companies in cases sentenced in Apr-May 2026, using deepfake-assisted interviews and stolen identities. Film has the MPA's Trusted Partner Network; games have no equivalent.
solution: A subscription 'passport' with five parts. (1) Contractor identity verification with liveness and injection-attack detection at onboarding and again at first privileged build access, tied to device posture. (2) A game-specific vendor security attestation, evidence-based (SSO, endpoint, repo hygiene) and shared across publishers so a vendor is assessed once. (3) Per-recipient forensic watermarking of builds, assets and design documents so a leak can be traced to a person or vendor. (4) Offboarding automation for contract end or layoff waves. (5) Insurer-ready evidence packages for cyber and E&O cover.
why_now: EA's leveraged buyout, Ubisoft's restructuring and Tencent-backed Vantage carve-out are all driving outsourcing. GTA VI's launch date will attract extortion attempts. North Korean IT-worker cases and deepfake interview kits make hiring-time identity checks insufficient. The IDScan.net breach (153M license scans) makes zero-retention verification a selling point (per briefing), and enterprise identity products are crowded but none focus on game supply chains.
revenue_model: Publishers pay $1.5-6k/month plus $30-80 per contractor-month. Vendors pay $200-500/month for a portable attestation badge, giving vendor-pays adoption. Watermarking priced per build distribution.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is not the publisher's own security but that each publisher re-audits the same few hundred vendors. A shared 'assess once, reuse everywhere' passport (film's TPN model) is cheaper for publishers and turns vendors into paying customers. Identity must be verified at the moment of privileged access rather than at hiring, because proxy interviews and deepfakes defeat interview-time checks.
first_30_days: Partner with 2-3 mid-size publishers or a co-dev/QA outsourcer. Draft a 40-question game-specific assessment, wire up an existing IDV API plus a device-posture check, and pilot with one outsourcing vendor. Offer a 'leak-trace drill' using watermarks on a demo build. Sell to publishers' security leads at $1.5k/month pilots.

title: Managed 24-Hour CRA Vulnerability Reporting Desk
one_liner: A hosted OWASP Dependency-Track plus an on-call analyst rota that tells small hardware makers within hours whether an exploited vulnerability hits their firmware, then drafts the ENISA 24h/72h filings.
customer: EU-selling makers of connected hardware with 5-250 staff and no product-security team (smart-home devices, e-bikes, EV chargers, industrial gateways, toys, wearables). Buyer is the CTO or regulatory/CE-marking manager. Secondary channel is CE-marking consultants who need a white-label reporting partner.
problem: The EU Cyber Resilience Act's reporting duties went live on 11 Sept 2026. Manufacturers must send an early warning within 24 hours of becoming aware of an actively exploited vulnerability, then detail within 72 hours, through ENISA's Single Reporting Platform. Fines reach EUR 15M or 2.5% of turnover. Small makers ship Yocto, OpenWrt, Zephyr, OpenSSL and FFmpeg stacks and often can't say what is inside a firmware image. Nobody on their team is awake on Sunday when a CISA KEV entry lands.
solution: Ingest CycloneDX/SPDX SBOMs into a managed Dependency-Track instance. For products with no SBOM, generate one from the firmware image with Syft, cdxgen or EMBA, using Ghidra for binary-only blobs. Watch CISA KEV, the EU vulnerability database and OSV continuously. A human analyst issues a VEX verdict (affected / not affected / under investigation) within hours. If affected, the desk pre-fills the SRP notification, drafts the customer advisory, and tracks the 24h, 72h and final-report clocks. The output is an auditable VEX history that a market-surveillance authority or notified body can read.
why_now: The 24-hour reporting clock started 11 Sept 2026 and the ENISA platform is open, so thousands of small makers are discovering they have weeks rather than the Dec 2027 date for full application. Dependency-Track and CycloneDX are the de facto open standards, but the paid options are enterprise appsec suites priced far above a 20-person hardware company's budget.
revenue_model: Retainer of EUR 300-1,500 per month per product family, tiered by number of firmware images and response-time SLA. One-off firmware SBOM generation at EUR 2-8k per image. Resale to CE consultants at a wholesale rate. Later add annual CRA technical-file support.
non_obvious_insight: Small manufacturers don't need another scanner, because the open-source plumbing already works. They need a human who can say 'not affected' with evidence inside 24 hours, because a false 'affected' filing is also costly. The scarce asset is analyst judgment plus a growing VEX history, which compounds across customers who share the same upstream components.
first_30_days: Stand up stock Dependency-Track and a KEV/EUVD watcher. Recruit 2-3 freelance embedded-security engineers for a shared on-call rota. Offer 20 free 'CRA exposure scans' (one firmware image in, one-page exposed-CVE report out) to IoT startups and to 100 CE-marking consultants found on LinkedIn and trade forums. Publish a weekly 'which exploited CVEs hit your Yocto/OpenWrt image' digest to build the list. Convert scans into 6-month retainers at a design-partner price.

title: Design-for-Duty: Engineer Below the 15% Metal Line
one_liner: A CAD/BOM tool that redesigns imported products to fall under Section 232's metal-weight cliffs or qualify for the 10% US-melt rate.
customer: Product-engineering and sourcing leads at $20M-$500M brands that import metal-heavy goods (furniture, fitness gear, grills, hand tools, lighting, enclosures, HVAC accessories).
problem: Since 2026-04-06 metals duties apply to full customs value: 50% on primary metal, 25% on derivatives, and 10% if made with US-melted steel or US-smelted aluminum/copper. Products under 15% metal weight are excluded (per Foley; verify current text). More derivative articles were proposed on 2026-08-06. Insiders treat this as a sourcing or lobbying problem. Brokers and freight forwarders cannot change a bill of materials, and engineers do not know the cliff exists.
solution: A plugin and standalone tool that ingests CAD mass properties and the BOM (SolidWorks, Fusion, Onshape or CSV). It computes metal weight share per SKU and simulates variants, such as a polymer or wood part in place of a steel bracket, or one US-melted component. It returns duty-weighted landed cost per variant and drafts the engineering change order. It also flags SKUs sitting just above a tier boundary.
why_now: The IEEPA tariffs fell on 2026-02-20 and the regime moved onto Section 232. Metal content is now the biggest variable in landed cost. Full-value duties began in April 2026, and the August 2026 proposal adds derivative products.
revenue_model: SaaS at $1.5-4k a month per product line. Launch-phase audits at $1.5k per SKU. Optional 10-15% share of first-year duty saved on redesigned SKUs.
non_obvious_insight: The tariff is a bill-of-materials problem, not a country problem. A few points of mass shifted can be worth more than moving a factory, and no one in the chain (broker, freight forwarder, sourcing agent) is paid to touch the design.
first_30_days: Pull public bill-of-lading data for HTS chapters exposed to metal derivatives. Cold-email 100 product heads offering a free one-SKU cliff check. Sell 10 fixed-price SKU audits at $1.5k, done in a spreadsheet. Retain a customs attorney to confirm how metal weight is measured. Build the plugin once patterns repeat.

title: Insurer-Billable Circles for GLP-1 Quitters
angle: Pairing 1: Healthcare delivery/GLP-1/longevity/consumer health x Mental health/loneliness/community/meaning
one_liner: Twelve-week therapist-and-dietitian-led groups for people coming off GLP-1s, funded through behavioral-health and nutrition benefits rather than 'weight loss' budgets.
customer: Employers and carriers that just dropped GLP-1 coverage (about 14% more plan to by 2027) and the ex-users themselves ($299 cash cohorts to start). GLP-1 telehealth firms are a later channel, as a retention add-on.
problem: Only about a third of non-diabetic patients are still on therapy at 1 year, and cost is the top reason. Stoppers regain weight about 4x faster than behavioral losers, roughly 60% of ex-users intend to restart, and 70% report lost joy in eating. Returning food noise, binge eating and body-identity distress get no clinical owner, because pharma, PBMs and telehealth are paid for volume or price, not persistence.
solution: Small cohorts of about 8 are co-led by a licensed therapist (CBT/ACT, binge-eating experience) and a registered dietitian. Content covers returning food noise, structured eating, protein and resistance-training basics, and a relapse plan. A partner prescriber offers a taper or low-cost maintenance plan (for example a $149 pill) and defines restart triggers. Where clinically indicated (BED, adjustment disorder), sessions bill as in-network group psychotherapy (CPT 90853) with dietitian MNT, using honest coding only. Employers can instead buy it as a $450-700 per-participant 'transition benefit'.
why_now: Employer GLP-1 coverage for weight loss fell from 72% to 60% in 2026 and more employers are dropping it before open enrollment now. Brand pill prices fell to $149-$299 cash, so 'restart cheaply' is a real option. The Medicare $50 Bridge copay ends Dec 2027, and JAMA Psychiatry 2026 found GLP-1 use of about 50% among binge-eating-disorder patients.
revenue_model: In-network group-therapy and MNT claims, or an employer per-participant fee ($450-700 per 12-week cohort versus about $12k a year for the drug), plus an optional $29-49 per month prescriber maintenance subscription.
non_obvious_insight: Employers cut coverage to save money and created a pool of abrupt discontinuers with no plan. The only bundle in this space that insurers already pay for by law is behavioral-health group care, so the funding path is mental-health parity, not obesity medicine. That also aligns with the psychological cause of regain (food noise, identity, bingeing) rather than another diet.
first_30_days: Sign one therapist with binge-eating experience and one RD, both credentialed through an existing group practice. Recruit the first cohort of 8 from GLP-1 subreddits and Facebook groups at $299 cash. Approach three mid-size employers through brokers who have just announced dropped coverage. Track 12-week weight regain, binge episodes and restart rates against a naive expectation.

title: Tender-Time Snapshots: Post-Montgomery Broker Defense File
one_liner: A tamper-evident, per-load record of exactly what a broker knew about a carrier at the moment of tender, built to survive plaintiff discovery and to satisfy underwriters, then upgraded into a placed contingent-liability program for small brokers.
customer: Independent brokerages and host-agency networks doing roughly $2M-$60M in gross revenue that buy contingent auto liability through a wholesaler. Secondary payers: MGAs, wholesalers and E&S carriers that now need underwriting evidence.
problem: On May 14, 2026 the Supreme Court unanimously held in Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II that negligent-hiring claims against brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA, so state-law suits now reach discovery. Insurance trade press (The Insurer, Sept 17, 2026, quoting RPS) is already calling it a capacity problem for broker contingent liability, and underwriters are asking for a paper trail of what was reviewed, when, and what was concluded. A small broker's carrier file is an onboarding PDF from 14 months ago plus email threads. Authority status, insurance, safety rating, ownership and contact info can change any day, and nobody can show what the screen said on the day of the load.
solution: Hook into tender events (TMS export, rate-con email forward, or load-board booking). At each tender, pull and hash-timestamp a snapshot: authority status, safety rating, insurance certificate validity, CSA/out-of-service rates, recent MCS-150 or contact-info changes, fraud flags, and which of the broker's own written selection rules the carrier passed. Any override is logged with a reason and the person who made it. A one-click 'selection file' export is formatted for a discovery request. Ship templates for a written carrier-selection standard drafted with trucking defense counsel. Phase 2: use the aggregated data to place small brokers into a wholesaler/MGA contingent-liability program with pricing credit for documented behavior.
why_now: Montgomery (May 14, 2026) removed the broad preemption defense. Contingent auto liability and E&O are repricing and capacity is tightening, per industry reporting in Sept 2026. The FMCSA broker financial-responsibility rule took full effect Jan 16, 2026, with suspension if security stays below $75K for 7 business days, so brokers cannot absorb a surprise verdict or claim.
revenue_model: SaaS at $0.50-$1.50 per tendered load or $300-$1,200/month by volume. Phase 2 adds a 10-15% commission on premium placed through the program, plus referral fees from defense firms.
non_obvious_insight: Plaintiffs' counsel does not ask 'did you vet the carrier?' They ask 'show me what your system showed at the minute you tendered, and who overrode it.' Brokers who vetted diligently at onboarding still lose, because they cannot prove tender-day state. Every broker knows the overrides happen at 4:45pm on a Friday when a load must be covered, and underwriters will price that override discipline. The record also proves the absence of red flags, which is the reasonable-care defense.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 small brokers through freight-broker Facebook groups and TIA chapters. Co-write a reasonable-care checklist with one trucking defense attorney. Build a snapshot logger on public FMCSA data plus an insurance-certificate check, ingesting tenders by CSV or forwarded rate-con emails so no TMS integration is needed. The sales hook is a free 'Discovery Fire Drill': simulate a plaintiff's request against the broker's last 5 loads and show the gaps. Convert at $299/month. In parallel, take the aggregate data to two wholesale brokers to test whether a premium credit is feasible.

title: Post-Divorce Beneficiary Cleanup for Family Lawyers
one_liner: Sell divorce attorneys a flat-fee sweep that finds and fixes stale beneficiary designations, since the will is the least important estate document.
customer: Family-law attorneys and divorce mediators or CDFAs. The initial buyer is the law firm, which adds it to the closing checklist. It expands later to advisors and benefits platforms.
problem: Most middle-class wealth passes by beneficiary designation (401(k)s, IRAs, life insurance, TOD/POD accounts), not by will. For ERISA plans the plan documents generally control even when the divorce decree says otherwise (Egelhoff v. Egelhoff, Kennedy v. Plan Administrator). Clients rarely update every form. Ex-spouses get paid, second families litigate, and the lawyer faces malpractice exposure.
solution: A 'Post-Decree Beneficiary Sweep'. The client links accounts or uploads statements. Software plus a paralegal gets each custodian's current designation, compares it to the decree, will and trust, and produces a discrepancy report. It prepares custodian-specific change forms for e-signature and tracks each until confirmed. A yearly re-audit subscription follows, triggered by life events (birth, remarriage, death).
why_now: Account aggregation and LLM extraction from messy statements and custodian PDFs now make cross-custodian paperwork cheap. Retirement balances sit at record levels, and divorce among the over-50s ('grey divorce') has risen for decades. The transfer wave is putting designation errors in the spotlight.
revenue_model: $295-$495 flat per divorce billed as a firm disbursement, $79/yr monitoring, and an enterprise license to benefits platforms and advisors at roughly $1-3 per participant per year.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone in estate planning talks about wills and trusts. The biggest mis-transfers happen through forms nobody re-reads. Divorce is the one moment when a lawyer, a deadline and malpractice fear are all in the room, so it is the cheapest place to sell an audit.
first_30_days: Sell to 10 solo and small family-law firms as a flat add-on. Process the first 20 cases manually with a paralegal and spreadsheet. Track the share of clients whose ex-spouse is still named anywhere (a hypothesis to measure) and turn that into a case study and a malpractice-avoidance pitch.

title: Kitchen Circuit Retrofit for India's Induction Switch
one_liner: Induction demand is real but low-income wiring cannot handle it, so sell the safe electrical retrofit and finance it.
customer: Lower-income urban households and resident welfare associations, reached through local electricians and hardware shops; discoms and state schemes can co-fund.
problem: After the LPG shortage, induction cooktop demand jumped 20-25x, the government is handing out 500k stoves, and the shift could add up to 27 GW. The Hindu reports low-income uptake is sluggish because of old wiring, overloaded meters and no financing.
solution: A pre-certified plug-and-play kit: dedicated 16A circuit, MCB/RCCB, heavy-duty socket and load-limiting smart plug, installed in two hours and paid in 12 EMIs. The wedge is 500 homes in one city through about 30 electricians.
why_now: The Hormuz energy shock created panic demand in March 2026, and the grid and household wiring are the binding constraint.
revenue_model: Rs 2,500-4,000 per kit and install at about 30% margin, plus an EMI spread and programme fees from discoms.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone counts stoves sold. The bottleneck is the last 15 metres of copper, and the first fire wave will turn certified retrofits into a regulated must-buy.
first_30_days: Design the kit with a licensed electrical engineer and pre-sell it through 20 electricians and one housing association.

title: Low-Background Human Data: Witnessed Creative Corpora
one_liner: Like pre-war steel, certifiably human creative work is becoming scarce, so sell fresh, witnessed, process-verified corpora to labs and detector vendors.
customer: AI labs and evaluation teams, detector vendors that need gold human test sets, and data-licensing brokers.
problem: Anything scraped from the web after 2023 is contaminated (AI is over 50% of Deezer daily uploads, and large shares of text are machine-made). Labs need uncontaminated creative data for evals, style diversity and fine-tuning. Detector vendors need known-human sets to measure false positives. No one can currently prove any given item is human.
solution: A paid panel of ID-verified writers, illustrators and musicians produce work under witnessed capture (screen and keystroke logs, DAW session logs, timelapse). Each item ships with process evidence in a quarterly dataset subscription. Creators are paid per item plus royalties from dataset revenue. Start with a 5,000-item 'human baseline' across text, illustration and music.
why_now: Contamination is now measurable, detector-scoring consequences are public, and human data has become a large market. Process-capture tooling for creative apps is cheap.
revenue_model: $25-300k per dataset subscription, per-item pricing of $5-200, and evaluation-as-a-service, with 50-60% of revenue to creators.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce good is not more data but certifiably unpolluted data, and every improvement in AI raises its price. The premium for 'guaranteed human' is set by buyers who cannot get it anywhere else.
first_30_days: Recruit 100 creators from paid-newsletter and Discord communities. Build a capture app (browser extension plus DAW logging). Send a sample data card to detector vendors and two labs' eval teams, and sell a $25-75k baseline set.

title: Canary Errors: Measure If Human Reviewers Still Catch Mistakes
one_liner: Phishing-simulation for 'human in the loop': plant known, harmless defects in AI drafts headed to human reviewers and sell the measured catch-rate as audit-grade proof of oversight.
customer: Risk, compliance, and legal-ops heads at 20-500 lawyer firms, medical-coding/RCM companies, claims-review shops, and AML/KYC alert-review BPOs. The malpractice and E&O carriers and brokers that cover them are the second payer and the distribution channel.
problem: Every AI risk policy ends with 'a human reviews it.' Nobody measures whether that human still catches errors. Automation bias means that as the AI gets 98% right, reviewers drift into rubber-stamping. Clients, insurers and regulators now ask for evidence of effective oversight. Lawyers have been sanctioned in hundreds of cases for fabricated AI citations, and Deloitte Australia refunded part of a government fee in 2025 over AI-hallucinated errors in a report. Firms can show that a review step exists but cannot show that it works.
solution: A thin layer between the AI draft and the reviewer: a Word/DMS plugin or queue middleware. It seeds a small percentage of items with synthetic, known-answer defects: swapped case citations, transposed numbers, altered party names, wrong ICD or CPT codes. Nothing seeded ever ships, because a defect the reviewer misses is caught by the system before release, and the reviewer gets an instant 'gotcha' micro-lesson. It records catch, miss and time per reviewer and per workflow, adapts difficulty, and outputs an 'Oversight Effectiveness Report' mapped to EU AI Act human-oversight duties, ISO 42001, SR 11-7 and client outside-counsel guidelines. The end state is a vigilance score that insurers can price against.
why_now: Agentic workflows in 2025-26 push more volume through single-click 'approve' steps. Courts and clients now punish unreviewed AI output. EU AI Act human-oversight obligations for high-risk systems are coming, even with the timeline under revision. Insurers launching AI-specific coverage (Lloyd's-backed products, AI-underwriting startups) have no data on whether human controls actually work.
revenue_model: Per-reviewer seat at $30-90/month; workflow-level enterprise licenses at $20-100k/yr; insurer-branded 'verified oversight' certificates. Later, a data partnership with carriers that gives premium credits for high catch-rates.
non_obvious_insight: The market treats human review as a binary control ('there is a human'), but it is a decaying skill: the better the AI, the worse the human vigilance, as with airline autopilot. Whoever owns the catch-rate dataset becomes the credit bureau of human oversight, and insurers will price off it. It is also a wedge into every regulated workflow, because seeding defects needs no access to the underlying model.
first_30_days: Build a .docx defect injector for contract and brief review (citation swaps, number transpositions, defined-term drift). Recruit 3 small firms or legal-ops teams and one legal-malpractice broker as design partners. Run a free two-week baseline audit on about 10 lawyers and publish an anonymized benchmark ('the average associate catches X% of seeded citation errors') for PR and inbound. Convert to $2-5k paid pilots.

title: Pooled Tariff-Surcharge Refund Claims for Small Buyers
one_liner: Connect to small businesses' accounting data, find tariff surcharges they paid distributors, and pool their claims against the same suppliers now receiving IEEPA refunds.
customer: Restaurants and restaurant groups, contractors, small manufacturers and retailers that bought through distributors who added tariff surcharge lines in 2025, paying on contingency.
problem: The Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs in February 2026, and CBP began taking refund claims through its CAPE portal on April 20, 2026, with roughly $175B owed to about 330,000 importers. Suppliers who passed the tariff through on itemized surcharges are now collecting refunds. Small buyers who paid those lines have claims but no visibility and no lawyer, since a $3k claim is uneconomic to pursue alone.
solution: Read 24 months of AP data (QuickBooks, Bill.com, email invoices) with an LLM to isolate itemized surcharges and post-tariff price jumps by supplier. Aggregate each supplier's small-buyer claims into one pooled demand or arbitration or class action through a partner consumer-protection firm. Track which suppliers have filed for refunds. Later, add econometric analysis of 'embedded' non-itemized price increases.
why_now: Refunds are being issued now (typically 60 to 90 days after acceptance), so the window for suppliers to hold and spend the money is short. Pass-through disputes have begun to appear in courts, but law firms focus on large B2B claimants. Litigation and CBP timing remains uncertain (the government appealed the refund order), which favors moving fast.
revenue_model: 20% to 30% contingency on recovered amounts, plus a fixed fee to run the AP analysis for larger buyers.
non_obvious_insight: Claims are tiny individually but concentrated by supplier. Two hundred restaurants that all bought from the same three distributors are a multimillion-dollar claim against three defendants. The supplier-level dataset (who added surcharges, when, how much, who filed) is the moat, and it is built one small customer at a time.
first_30_days: Build a free 'surcharge finder' that scans an uploaded invoice export or QuickBooks connection and shows what was paid. Recruit through restaurant and contractor associations and bookkeepers. Sign 50 claimants on contingency and target the 10 distributors whose surcharges show up most often. Line up a partner litigation firm.

title: Security Grant Desk for Small Congregations
one_liner: Flat-fee application, vulnerability-assessment and post-award compliance packages for small houses of worship using FEMA's Nonprofit Security Grant Program and state equivalents.
customer: Small synagogues, mosques, churches, gurdwaras and temples, and umbrella bodies such as federations, dioceses and mosque councils.
problem: FY2026 NSGP offered $300M (notice published 24 June 2026, deadline extended to 24 July) at up to $200k per site. Applications need a vulnerability assessment, an investment justification and SAM.gov and UEI registration. Small congregations lack the administrative capacity, and post-award procurement and reimbursement rules trip them.
solution: Templated assessments built on CISA's free self-assessment, an investment-justification drafting workflow with security-vendor quote gathering, SAM and UEI onboarding, a state-agency deadline tracker, and post-award procurement and reimbursement compliance. Flat fees only, because FEMA guidance generally bars contingent-fee grant writing.
why_now: FY2026 awards are being announced now and FY2027 prep starts this fall. Threat levels keep congregations motivated.
revenue_model: $1.5-4k per application, $800 for post-award compliance, and $150/month trackers for federations.
non_obvious_insight: The barrier is administrative capacity, not eligibility, and referrals flow through community federations. Post-award compliance is the neglected second revenue stream.
first_30_days: Partner with 2 regional federations or mosque councils, run free FY2027-prep webinars, and sell 10 assessment packages. Build a network of vetted security installers for quotes.

title: Licensed Local-Language Speech Data Exchange
one_liner: Pay radio stations and call centers for rights-cleared audio and resell it to the voice-AI builders who cannot get it anywhere else.
customer: Voice-AI startups and model labs that need low-resource African and Indian language audio; radio stations and telco call centers are the suppliers.
problem: Foreign APIs are unusable for local voice because of latency and jitter. Startups like AethexAI train small models on call-center recordings and radio audio, but rights, cleaning and transcription are ad hoc.
solution: A consented, speaker-anonymised and transcribed archive with clear licences and revenue share for stations. The wedge is 3-5 stations in one language (Hausa, Yoruba or Swahili), with a sample set for a paying pilot.
why_now: 300M-1.7B parameter voice models now work in production, and Intron covers 57 languages. Labs face scrutiny over scraped data, and Sarvam and AethexAI are raising money.
revenue_model: $20-80 per cleaned, licensed hour, with 40-50% shared with the station, plus annual subscriptions.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders assume low-resource data is unsellable because the markets are poor. The buyers are well-funded labs, and rights-cleared audio, not raw audio, is the bottleneck.
first_30_days: Sign three stations, digitise about 2,000 hours and clean 200 as a sample. Sell a paid pilot dataset to one voice-AI startup.

title: PFAS Land-Application History Reports for Farmland
one_liner: A 'Phase I environmental site assessment' for PFAS on farmland, built from biosolids land-application records and upstream discharger data, sold to lenders, farmland funds and appraisers before the sensors exist.
customer: Farm Credit associations and ag banks, farmland investment funds, rural appraisers and title firms, and farmers or buyers who need to show a field is clean.
problem: EPA released Draft Guidance for Reducing Risk from PFOA and PFOS in Biosolids on July 1, 2026, noting that sewage sludge may carry PFAS from industrial dischargers, landfills and homes. Yet EPA's own FY2026 SBIR Phase I topics still ask small businesses to invent 'Treatment of PFAS in Wastewater Sewage Sludge and Biosolids' and 'Sensors to Detect PFAS in Environmental Matrices', so cheap field screening does not exist. Lenders and buyers are pricing farmland today with no way to know whether a field received sludge, from which plant, and with what upstream industrial inputs.
solution: A desktop screening report per parcel. It combines state biosolids land-application permits and site reports (obtained by scraping and automated public-records requests), the treatment plant's upstream industrial dischargers, soil and hydrology data, and a risk tier. Higher tiers trigger a sampling plan run by a partner lab using EPA Method 1633. Deliver in the lender's existing environmental-diligence workflow, and later offer an API.
why_now: The July 1, 2026 EPA draft guidance turns PFAS in biosolids from a research topic into something lenders must ask about. EPA's Sept 24, 2026 SBIR solicitation ($100k per Phase I, 6 months, closes Nov 8, 2026) is paying for the sensing tools, so cheap field tests are years away and records-based screening is the only option now.
revenue_model: $400 to $1,200 per desktop parcel report. $2k to $6k with coordinated sampling (margin on lab work). $20k to $60k per year API or portfolio subscriptions for lenders and farmland funds.
non_obvious_insight: The government is paying to invent PFAS sensors that don't exist yet, but the lend/buy/insure decision is being made now on paper records, so the winning product is the record-linkage layer, not the sensor. EPA's FY2026 SBIR Phase I topics list 1B (PFAS in sewage sludge and biosolids) and 2A (PFAS sensors in environmental matrices), $100,000 and 6 months each: https://www.epa.gov/sbir/how-apply-sbir-contract. EPA's biosolids page lists the July 1, 2026 Draft Guidance and states that sludge may carry PFAS from upstream dischargers: https://www.epa.gov/biosolids. Lenders already require site assessments for gas stations and dry cleaners, and a PFAS-on-farmland version is the missing sibling. Caveat: the EPA pages I could fetch gave no land-application tonnage or state-by-state record availability, so records access must be checked before committing to a state.
first_30_days: Pick 1 or 2 states where biosolids land-application permits are public (verify first). Assemble records for the 20 largest treatment plants and build 25 sample reports on real parcels. Approach 5 Farm Credit associations, 3 farmland funds and 5 rural appraisers with a free report on a parcel they already own or are underwriting. Sign a lab partner for sampling. Close the first 3 paid pilots at $400 to $1,200 per parcel.

title: Mitigation Grant Packets for Small Towns
one_liner: A packet factory and compliance tracker that gets small governments through FEMA and state mitigation grants without clawbacks.
customer: Municipalities under 25,000 people, counties, tribal governments, special districts and state emergency-management agencies, paid from management-cost lines.
problem: BRIC was cancelled in April 2025, restored by court order, reinstated Mar 18 2026 with $1B, and applications closed July 23 2026. Small governments lack staff for benefit-cost analysis, environmental and historic review, procurement and match documentation, and then risk clawbacks. California's new Safe Homes Grant and SB 894 revolving loan need local administration.
solution: Standardized templates for the top project types (culvert upsizing, generators, elevation, defensible space, floodproofing, safe rooms), covering benefit-cost analysis, environmental checklists and procurement. Add post-award compliance and drawdown tracking, built for several programs since BRIC timing is uncertain.
why_now: Federal funding restarted but is unstable. States are building their own programs, and big consultants ignore small jobs.
revenue_model: $6-20K fixed fee per packet and $1-2K/month compliance retainers.
non_obvious_insight: Government grants are gated by paperwork, and the volume of unserved demand sits in towns that big consultants skip.
first_30_days: Cold-email 200 town managers in high-hazard states with a free readiness scan, and sign 3 pilots.
